output.executive_summary: The brief reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025 examining the relationship between tree canopy and afternoon land-surface temperature. After accounting for impervious surfaces and building density, each 10-percentage-point increase in canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature; impervious surface was the strongest single predictor [S1][S2][S3]. The authors recommend prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035, with an estimated cost of about $2.1 million over ten years for 6,000 street trees [S4]. The brief cautions that land-surface temperature is not air temperature and that its cross-sectional findings show association, not causation [S4].
output.detailed_summary:
The September 2026 brief by Dr. Amara Nwosu and Kenji Morita of the Riverton Institute for Urban Studies summarizes research on 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. It reports that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief presents these findings as support for targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods [S1].

For the analysis, canopy cover was measured from 2024 aerial imagery and ranged from 6% to 41% across the neighborhoods. Land-surface temperature (LST) was derived from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, all between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. A multiple regression model used average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors [S2].

Eastgate, with 6% canopy, was the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C; Willow Park, with 41% canopy, was the coolest, averaging 34.8°C. The difference was 6.4°C. Share of impervious surface was the strongest single predictor of surface temperature, followed by canopy cover. Heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile [S3].

The brief notes that LST is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design establishes association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. It recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. The authors estimate that planting 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years [S4].

key_findings.text: Each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density.
Canopy cover ranged from 6% to 41% across the 48 neighborhoods; Eastgate averaged 41.2°C and Willow Park averaged 34.8°C, a difference of 6.4°C.
Share of impervious surface was the strongest single predictor of surface temperature, and canopy cover was the second strongest.
Heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile.

output.executive_summary: The Catalog Modernization Project is reported as Amber: it remains on schedule for the planned November 17, 2026 go-live, but its forecast cost is $6,500 above the approved budget, mainly due to additional data-cleanup work [S1][S2]. By September 30, 2026, 412,000 of 485,000 catalog records had been migrated, and data mapping, the Central branch pilot, and usability testing of the new search interface were completed [S1]. The steering committee approved extending the pilot to Eastgate and Millbrook, while staff training remains in progress [S2]. The report identifies duplicate records and a vendor staffing change as risks, and lists actions with October deadlines, including confirming contingency funding [S3].
output.detailed_summary:
The report covers July 1 to September 30, 2026, and was prepared by Elena Vasquez, Project Manager, Harbor City Public Library; its report date is October 6, 2026. Overall status is Amber. The project is described as on schedule for go-live but over budget. Data migration is 85% complete, with 412,000 of 485,000 catalog records migrated to the new platform provided by Larkspur Data Services LLC. Go-live is planned for November 17, 2026, when public access to the legacy catalog will also end [S1].

Quarterly highlights include completion of data mapping on July 24, 2026, completion of the pilot migration at the Central branch on August 28, 2026, and successful usability testing of the new patron search interface with 18 volunteer patrons [S1]. The approved budget is $180,000; spending was $112,400 as of September 30, 2026, and the forecast at completion is $186,500, or $6,500 over budget, mainly because of additional data-cleanup work [S2]. The milestones list data mapping and pilot migration as complete, staff training as in progress, and go-live as planned for November 17, 2026. The report also includes a milestone marked “Due” with the date November 3, 2026, but does not identify its milestone name [S2].

On September 9, 2026, the steering committee approved extending the pilot to two additional branch libraries, Eastgate and Millbrook [S2]. The report identifies a risk that duplicate bibliographic records from the legacy system may delay go-live. Tomas Lindqvist, Data Lead, owns this risk; the stated mitigation is to run a deduplication script by October 20, 2026. A second risk is that Larkspur's lead migration engineer is leaving the vendor in November 2026; the project has requested a written staffing transition plan from Larkspur [S3].

The listed action items are for Elena Vasquez to circulate the revised staff training schedule by October 10, 2026; Tomas Lindqvist to deliver the deduplication report by October 20, 2026; and Finance to confirm contingency funding of $6,500 by October 31, 2026 [S3].

output.overview: Amendment No. 1 changes several terms of the Master Services Agreement effective July 1, 2026: the monthly service fee, non-renewal notice period, and availability commitment. It also adds an accessibility-reporting obligation. The amendment states that all other terms remain unchanged and that it prevails in case of conflict.

findings.description: Both documents identify Larkspur Data Services LLC as Provider and Harbor City Public Library as Client; the amendment identifies the Master Services Agreement dated March 1, 2025 as the agreement it amends. [S1] [S5]

The Agreement sets the monthly service fee at $4,500.00 and says fees are fixed for the initial term, with fee changes requiring a written amendment signed by both parties. [S2] The amendment changes Section 3.1 to $5,200.00 effective July 1, 2026, to cover hosting and support of the digital archive module. [S5] This is a stated amendment, rather than an unexplained contradiction.
The Agreement requires written non-renewal notice at least sixty (60) days before the end of the current term. [S1] The amendment changes this period to ninety (90) days. [S5]

The Agreement sets the monthly availability target at 99.5%. [S3] The amendment raises it to 99.9% and states that the existing Section 5.2 service-credit mechanism applies to the new target. [S5] [S6]

The amendment adds a new Section 11 requiring a quarterly accessibility audit report of the public catalog against WCAG 2.2 Level AA within fifteen (15) days after each calendar quarter ends. The Agreement excerpt contains no corresponding reporting obligation. [S3] [S4] [S6]

The amendment says all Agreement terms not amended remain unchanged and in force, and that the amendment prevails if it conflicts with the Agreement. [S7] The listed changes address Sections 2.2, 3.1, and 5.1 and add Section 11; the other provisions shown in the Agreement are not identified as changed. [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5] [S6]

output.limitations: The supplied Agreement excerpts do not show the full text of every section, and the amendment does not reproduce the complete amended sections. The comparison therefore relies on the text provided and does not assess unstated terms.

output.overview: Both documents describe the Catalog Modernization Project, report an approved budget of $180,000 and a forecast at completion of $186,500, and identify a $6,500 forecast overrun. The finance memo updates spending with a later as-of date and adds a December schedule assumption, a payment detail, and an unresolved question about training costs. Its December 1 go-live assumption differs from the status report’s November 17 planned go-live date; the documents do not explain the difference.

findings.description: Both documents state an approved budget of $180,000 and a forecast at completion of $186,500, which is $6,500 above budget. [S2] [S4]

The status report gives spending to date as $112,400 as of September 30, 2026, while the finance memo gives $118,900 as of October 10, 2026. The figures have different as-of dates, so the difference is contextual rather than a contradiction. [S2] [S4]

The status report says the planned go-live date remains November 17, 2026, while the finance memo’s schedule assumes go-live on December 1, 2026. The documents do not say whether the project date changed or why finance uses a different assumption. [S1] [S5]

The finance memo states that a final implementation installment of $9,000.00 is payable to Larkspur in December 2026. The status report does not provide an installment amount or payment timing. [S2] [S5]

The finance memo asks whether staff training costs of $7,800 are included in the $186,500 forecast at completion; the status report gives the forecast but does not address whether training costs are included. [S2] [S5]

The status report lists confirmation of $6,500 in contingency funding by October 31, 2026 as an action item. The later finance memo recommends that the steering committee approve $6,500 from the technology reserve to cover the forecast overrun; it does not state that the funding has been approved. [S3] [S4]

The status report provides project execution details: migration is 85% complete (412,000 of 485,000 records), the project is on schedule but over budget, and it describes milestones, risks, and branch-pilot expansion. The finance memo focuses on budget and schedule assumptions and does not report those operational details. [S1] [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5]

output.limitations: The documents do not explain the difference between the November 17, 2026 planned go-live date and the December 1, 2026 finance assumption, or establish whether the forecast includes the $7,800 in staff training costs. The status report’s milestone table includes a date of November 3, 2026, but the associated milestone label is unclear in the supplied text.
